chapter_theme: The Govindaiyar ilampakam closes: Civakan is welcomed home after the herd's recovery, and the herd chief Nandagon, telling in confidence how the old king fell and how he himself turned back from suicide in hope that the line survived, offers his daughter Govindai with gold and the herd's wealth and argues from the gods that lineage is no bar; Civakan, holding that a man must first marry a woman of his own rank, accepts her for his friend Padumukan, and the herders' wedding is told in dairy rites and a bridegroom's unbounded pleasure.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by the merchant Kantukkatan
the merchant who raised Civakan, his foster father
the women of the city who welcome Civakan with the auspicious objects
the herd chief, father of Govindai, who names himself Govindan in 477
Civakan's friend, for whom he accepts Govindai
the herdsmen of the royal herds
the herdswomen of the cattle hamlets

472.reading: A thousand and eight women with flower garlands, their upper cloths slipping and ornaments ringing, carry the eight auspicious things and lead the young hero into his house.
472.event: Women bearing the eight auspicious objects escort Civakan home after the herd's recovery.
472.nuance: The welcome continues the procession of 470-471; the number ஆயிரத்தெண்மர் repeats the thousand and eight of the auspicious marks, a ritual figure rather than a count.

473.reading: His foster father, more to him than a mother, comes out to receive the youth of the shining spear and takes him in with care, as if Indra's son had come to the high world, and then, the verse says, the noble one speaks these words.
473.event: Kantukkatan receives Civakan at the house and guards him.
473.nuance: The closing formula தோன்றன்மற் றின்ன கூறும் is repeated word for word at the end of 474, which introduces Nandagon's speech; no speech of the father follows here, so either the formula belongs to 474 alone or a speech has been lost. Whether தோன்றல் here is the father or Civakan is not clear.

474.reading: The noble lord who rules the great herds, seeing the bountiful hero whose broad chest Fortune of the lotus embraces, speaks these words.
474.event: Nandagon, the herd chief, comes before Civakan and begins to speak.
474.nuance: The herd chief is named by his office (தொறுவை யாளும்), not by name; the name comes from his own mouth in 477.

475.reading: Nandagon asks Civakan to hear and then forget what he tells: the king of this land, who first brought ruin on himself, desired Vijayai, laid the whole burden of rule on Kattiyankaran, and by that man was crushed at the root of his fortune.
475.event: Nandagon recounts in confidence how Saccandan handed his rule to Kattiyankaran for love of Vijayai and was destroyed by him.

claims.claim: a king who hands his rule to another out of desire for his queen brings about his own ruin

475.nuance: Nandagon blames the king's own choice (முதற் கேடு சூழ்ந்த, 'who first plotted the ruin') and says nothing of a former deed, whereas the narrator at 215 says a destiny formed before sprouted in the king; the epic keeps both causes, in two voices. The irony, which the hero cannot yet share, is that the listener is the dead king's son. பொறிமுதல் may be 'fortune at its root' or point to the machine (பொறி) of the peacock flight; the sense of line 4 is not certain.

476.reading: Nandagon says that when the sceptre fell he climbed a high peak meaning to throw himself down and end his life, resolving to die if no heir of the great line survived, but thinking of the banyan seed he drew back from destruction.
476.event: Nandagon tells how, at the king's fall, he went to kill himself and turned back in hope that the royal line survived.
476.nuance: The banyan seed (ஆலம்வித்து) is the tiny seed of a vast tree: his hope is that one surviving child of the line could regrow the house. மால்வழி is read here as 'the great line'; it could be taken otherwise, and the sense of line 3 turns on it. The servant's loyal suicide is withheld, not condemned.

477.reading: Nandagon names himself: he comes of a family in the service of the king whose line ended with him, he lives among the herds and is called Govindan, and his wife, who came swift as the Godavari, bore the girl called Govindai.
477.event: Nandagon names himself and his daughter Govindai.
477.nuance: The daughter's name is formed from the father's. 'The king who ended with his clan' is what Nandagon believes of Saccandan; 476 has just shown him hoping it is not so.

478.reading: Nandagon says that his young daughter's bold glance went into men's hearts like a pressed-in arrow, and that among all his people who begged for the slender girl and suffered he stood with his smile gone.
478.nuance: Line 4 can also be read of the herd's loss before the raid was undone (நம்படை, 'our men', who had stood beaten); the reading here takes it of the suitors among his own people whom he could not satisfy.

479.reading: Nandagon offers Civakan the girl of the golden anklets and bangled wrists together with seven statues of fine gold, and asks him to join her in an unfailing wedding as her bridegroom.
479.event: Nandagon offers Govindai to Civakan in marriage with seven golden statues.
479.nuance: This keeps the proclamation of 440, that the maiden would go to whoever brought back the herd; the seven golden statues are added here.

480.reading: Nandagon praises his daughter in the goods of the herd: her sweetness wells like butter, her speech is sweet as the cream of milk, her body is like melted ghee, and her two eyes are karuvilam flowers.
480.nuance: The metre changes here for three verses (480-482). The herdsman's similes are all dairy: the poet gives him the idiom of his trade, as the Sangam mullai poems give it to herders.

481.reading: Nandagon promises to fill the underworld with the ghee of red cows, sweet milk and thick curd, and asks Civakan to garland his handmaid with flowers, knowing all that must follow.
481.event: Nandagon presses his offer with a promise of boundless dairy wealth.
481.nuance: He calls his daughter உன் அடிச்சி, 'your servant woman', offering her below the hero's station before the hero raises the question of rank in 483.

482.reading: Nandagon tells Civakan not to think of lineage: fragrant-garlanded Murukan enjoyed the beauty of Valli, and the husband of the Earth took the sweet nectar of the lips of Nappinnai of the long herds.

claims.claim: difference of lineage should not bar a marriage, since gods wed a hill girl and a herd girl

482.nuance: Both precedents are gods who married beneath them by birth: Valli is a hunter's daughter and Nappinnai a herdsman's. The father argues from myth, not from doctrine, and the argument is his own interest.

483.reading: Civakan reflects that men do not first unite with women unequal to them in birth before they have married a maiden of their own high lineage, and that this is the rule for men.
483.event: Civakan considers the offer and decides it would breach the order of marriage for him to take Govindai first.

claims.claim: a man of high birth should not marry a woman of unequal birth before he has married one of his own rank

483.nuance: This is the hero's thought, not his speech. It does not deny 482 that unequal marriage is possible; it orders it, so that rank governs which wife comes first. Lines 1-2 are hard to construe and the reading follows their sense with lines 3-4.

484.reading: Civakan, like a young tusker, looks at Nandagon and says, so as to cool his heart, that the girl is to be the crest and garland of one dear to him, and asks whether it is fitting to delay with such speeches.
484.event: Civakan accepts the offer and urges that the marriage be made without delay.
484.nuance: The sense turns on மாமான் in line 2, a kinship word whose referent is not clear; 489 shows that he accepts Govindai on behalf of Padumukan, and the reading takes the line in that light.

485.reading: The herd chief, in his wreath of honeyed mullai and red cloth, goes off in great joy into the crowd where curd is churned and orders that the wedding be performed in the pavilion of mayilai ringed with jasmine.
485.event: Nandagon orders the wedding to be held in the herders' pavilion.

486.reading: The women bring the girl, whose brow outdid Kama's bow and whose kuvalai eyes outdid the kayal fish, her anklets crying out, and set her down with praise.
486.event: The herdswomen bring Govindai to the pavilion.
486.nuance: Line 3 (இனியுளர் அல்லர் ஆயர்) seems to give the anklets' cry that the herders are 'no longer' something to her, perhaps that she now passes out of her people; the sense is not clear.

487.reading: The herdswomen dip in ghee, in a measure, grass the young cow's calf has eaten from, bless her to grow old with her husband age after age like cow and stall, pour ghee on her head and bathe her with water from a ladle.
487.event: The herdswomen perform the herders' bridal anointing and bathing of Govindai.
487.nuance: The rite is wholly of the herd: calf-grazed grass, ghee, a blessing in the image of cattle. Line 2's comparison (ஆவும் தோழும்) is read as cow and stall; it may be cow and bull.

488.reading: They take off the gold ear studs bought with ghee and the gem pendants, fasten the auspicious bridal thread, put on a garland and sandal paste, and make her a small simple adornment, and the herdswomen stand amazed.
488.event: The herdswomen adorn Govindai for the wedding.
488.nuance: நெய்விலைப் பசும்பொன், 'gold bought at the price of ghee', marks the herders' wealth as dairy wealth. The small adornment (சிறுபுன் கோலம்) is plain, yet it amazes the herdswomen themselves.

489.reading: As the drums sound the herders take her and go through the festive old town, and Nandagon, holding the pitcher, pours its water, which the hero receives, saying it is for prince Padumukan of the spear.
489.event: Nandagon gives Govindai by pouring water, and Civakan receives the gift on behalf of his friend Padumukan.
489.nuance: The pouring of water seals the gift of the bride; the giver's promise in 440 is kept, but the winner passes the prize to his friend. ஏறங்கோண் in line 1 is unclear; it may name horns or the bull-catch drums of the herders.

490.reading: Nandagon gives her two thousand young cows and the seven fine golden statues, and then Padumukan, struck by the sharp arrows of Kama's army, embraces her pearl-adorned breasts.
490.event: Nandagon gives the dowry and Padumukan is united with Govindai.

491.reading: Drinking without tiring the nectar of her sharp teeth, whose eyes are like paired kazhuneer flowers and whose garland is fragrant, the garlanded spearman falls into a sea of pleasure that cannot be contained.

492.reading: Wondering whether she is the nectar the gods churned from the sweet ocean of milk or a daughter of the herders, while the girl melts, Padumukan becomes one with no awareness left but of his unguarded pleasure.
492.event: Padumukan is lost in love for Govindai.
492.nuance: ஓம்பா ஒழுக்கத்து உணர்வொன்றிலன் can mean he kept no guard on himself or that he lost every awareness but this one; the narrator does not blame him. The nectar churned from the milk ocean answers the dairy similes of 480: the herd girl is made the gods' amrita.

links.note: At 215 the narrator says the king ignored counsel because a destiny formed before sprouted in him; Nandagon, telling the same fall, blames only the king's own desire and choice.
links.teaches: The epic keeps two causes for Saccandan's fall in two voices, so a former deed in the narrator's account never excuses the choice his subject remembers.

links.note: Nandagon turned back from suicide hoping, like a banyan seed, that the royal line survived; the patikam at 26 has Civakan spread his just sceptre over the land.
links.teaches: The cowherd's private hope is the plan of the whole epic, and he states it to the very heir he thinks may be lost.

links.note: The Naladiyar says that when a banyan is eaten hollow its aerial roots hold it up, as a son covers a weakened father; Nandagon's banyan seed is the hope that a son of the fallen king lives.
links.teaches: Set beside the quatrain, the herdsman's seed image takes on the son's work of propping a fallen house, which the epic will make a war for a kingdom rather than a household's shame.

gains.a: the obscure seed image is given its point: a hidden son is the root that will hold the line up
gains.b: the household maxim is seen stretched to a dynasty, where the father is dead and the son does not yet know whom he props

links.note: Nandagon argues from Murukan and Vishnu that lineage should not be thought of in marriage; Civakan at once thinks that a man may not take an unequal wife before one of his own rank.
links.teaches: The hero answers the herdsman's mythic precedent not by denying unequal marriage but by ranking it, so birth still governs the order of wives in a story that lets him marry across it.

links.note: The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Civakan holds that birth decides which wife a man may take first.
links.teaches: The pair shows the Kural's levelling of birth stopping at the threshold of marriage in the epic, where rank of birth remains a rule of conduct even for a hero honoured for his deeds.

gains.a: the hero's private rule is seen against a classic denial that birth confers worth, which makes its reliance on birth visible
gains.b: the couplet's claim is tested on a case it does not name, the ordering of marriages, where birth kept a force the couplet does not grant it

links.note: At 440 Nandagon had it proclaimed that the maiden would be given to whoever brought back the herd; at 479 he offers her to Civakan, adding seven golden statues.
links.teaches: The proclamation is kept to the letter, yet the hero's decline at 483-484 shows the prize could be honoured only by being passed to another.

links.note: Civakan's acceptance in 484 turns on an obscure kinship word; at 489 he receives the gift water on behalf of Padumukan.
links.teaches: Read from 489, Civakan's quick acceptance was always an acceptance for his friend, which lets him keep both Nandagon's honour and his own rule of rank.

links.note: In the Kalittokai the herd girl is cried as the prize of whoever takes the fighting bull, and the taker himself has her; here the herd chief's daughter is the prize for recovering the herd, and the winner passes her to a friend.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the mullai custom of a herd girl won by a public feat, but moves the feat from the herders' bull-pen to a prince's war and lets the prize be transferred, which the bull-catch, where the girl goes to the man who wrestled, does not allow.

gains.a: the herders' wedding is seen to rest on an old custom of the herd girl as prize of a feat, which explains the father's proclamation in 440
gains.b: the bull-catch's bond between feat and husband is shown to be what a later courtly telling could loosen, the girl becoming a gift between men

links.note: The couplet says the pleasure of love is a sea but its pain, when it strikes, is greater; 491 gives the bridegroom the sea of pleasure that cannot be contained, and no pain.
links.teaches: The epic uses the couplet's measure of pleasure as a sea but leaves out the greater sea of pain that the woman in the Kural speaks from, because the wedding has no separation in it.

gains.a: the uncontained sea of 491 is seen to be half of a measure, the half that a married union can claim
gains.b: the couplet's first clause is given a scene where it stands alone, which shows its second clause belongs to separation

links.note: At 216 Saccandan drinks unwearied the nectar of Vijayai and his fall begins; at 491-492 Padumukan drinks Govindai's nectar and loses all awareness in unguarded pleasure.
links.teaches: The poet gives the bridegroom the very image of the king whose drinking cost him his kingdom, so the epic's warning about pleasure lies under even its happiest wedding, though the narrator blames no one here.

new_concepts.gloss: the wedding; the rite that makes a marriage

source_issues: Verses 473 and 474 end with the same speech formula (தோன்றன்மற் றின்ன கூறும்), but only 474 is followed by a speech; 473's formula may be doubled from 474, or a speech of Civakan's foster father may be lost.
Verse 488 line 2 is a repaired line (TSCII slip, ோ் read as ேர்); the repair gives சேர்த்தி, which fits the sense.
Verses 480-482 are in a different, shorter metre from the surrounding viruttams; the text gives no rubric for the change.
Verse 489 line 1 ஏறங்கோண் is obscure as divided and may be corrupt or misdivided.

Cast id for the usurping minister differs across this book's chapter files (kattiyankaran in ch010 and ch019, kattiyangaran in ch011, ch012 and ch020); this chapter names him only in Nandagon's speech and does not cast him.
